clue.text: Satisfied, coming back with point for draw

indicators.note: something coming back travels the opposite way, so the word for satisfied is read from right to left

parts.note: met, as a need or demand is met
PT is the standard abbreviation for point

explanation.surface: A contented sports fan coming back from a game where a single point earned a draw.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Draw' looks like a tied match, but here it is a verb meaning to lure.
explanation.definitionFit: To draw someone in is to lure or attract them, which is what tempting does.

clue.text: Characters in party pessimistic

indicators.note: the answer sits in the following words, running across the gap between them

parts.note: the end of party joined to the start of pessimistic

explanation.surface: The people at a party are a gloomy lot.
explanation.definitionFit: Typed letters are characters, and a person described as a type is a character too.

clue.text: Broadcast learned item on prolific actress

indicators.note: broadcast seed is scattered in all directions, so the letters land in a new order

parts.note: the eleven letters to be rearranged
rich, as in abundant or productive

explanation.surface: A radio programme airs a scholarly piece about a hugely productive film star.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'on' means placed after, so RICH follows the rearranged letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Marlene Dietrich was a German-American film star and singer of the 1930s to 1950s.

clue.text: Philosopher after time studied boring routine

indicators.note: the philosopher comes after the other two pieces in the final word

parts.note: T is the abbreviation for time
to read a subject is to study it at university
John Stuart Mill, the English philosopher

explanation.surface: A philosopher, having studied for some time, finds it all a boring routine.
explanation.definitionFit: A treadmill is a monotonous round of work, from the wheel once turned endlessly by prisoners.

clue.text: Silly sailor with singular language, mostly

indicators.note: mostly means not all of it, so the language loses its final letter

parts.note: AB, able seaman
S is the grammatical abbreviation for singular
Urdu, a language of Pakistan and India

explanation.surface: A daft sailor who speaks an odd language, more or less.
explanation.definitionFit: Absurd means ridiculous or foolish, the same sense as silly.

clue.text: Confident president covering misfortune up

indicators.note: the president's name covers, or wraps around, the other word

parts.note: George Bush, father or son, US president

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means read from the bottom, so the word for misfortune runs backwards

parts.note: an ill is a misfortune or harm

explanation.surface: A self-assured president hushes up a mishap.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue the misfortune is read upwards before the president's name wraps round it.
explanation.definitionFit: Bullish describes optimistic, assertive confidence, as of a market expected to rise.

clue.text: Tip over unexpected result

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to knock something over
second meaning: a surprise win by the underdog

explanation.surface: A tipster's favoured horse going over a fence brings a surprise result.
explanation.definitionFit: To upset a vase is to overturn it, and in sport an upset is a shock defeat of the favourite.

clue.text: Leave coach, crossing street and beginning to explore large shop

parts.note: to depart is to leave

indicators.note: the coach is crossed through the middle by the street, which ends up inside it

parts.note: a mentor coaches a younger colleague
St is the abbreviation for street

indicators.note: only the first letter of the following word is wanted

parts.note: the first letter of explore

explanation.surface: Get off the bus, cross the road and go off to look round a big shop.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Coach' reads as a bus; it is a trainer. The street sits just before the trainer's last two letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A department store is a large retail shop divided into sections selling different goods.

clue.text: Rotten plonk, free

parts.note: to plonk something down is to put it there carelessly
to rid is to free

explanation.surface: Cheap wine that has gone off, and is given away for nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plonk' looks like cheap wine but works as a verb. A word for free follows it.
explanation.definitionFit: Putrid means decomposing and foul-smelling, as rotten food is.

clue.text: Spirit in TV network that surprises me!

indicators.note: the spirit is placed inside the name of the network

parts.note: CBS, the American television network
rum is a spirit made from sugar cane

explanation.surface: A viewer reacts to a ghost appearing on a television channel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spirit' suggests a ghost, but it is a drink. Crumbs is a mild British exclamation of surprise.
explanation.definitionFit: The interjection is said when something is mildly surprising, much like 'goodness me'.

clue.text: Constant favourite in nation, a leader in legend

indicators.note: the favourite is placed inside the name of the country

parts.note: Peru, the South American country
a pet is a favourite, as a teacher's pet
taken as written

indicators.note: the leader of a word is its first letter

parts.note: the first letter of legend

explanation.surface: A national hero leads the legend, always the favourite.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leader' looks like a national leader, but it only asks for the first letter of 'legend'.
explanation.definitionFit: Perpetual means never ending or continuous, as constant does.

clue.text: Fantastic agent, American, going west

indicators.note: in an across clue, west is leftwards, so the letters run from right to left

parts.note: a rep, short for representative, acts as an agent
US for American

explanation.surface: A brilliant American spy heads out to the West.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Going west' suggests a frontier story; it is the setter's way of saying the letters go leftwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Super is a colloquial word of praise meaning excellent or wonderful.

clue.text: Second mortgage provider perhaps inadequate

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for second
a bank or building society lending for a house is one example of a lender

explanation.surface: A second mortgage company may not give enough money.
explanation.definitionFit: Slender means meagre or scanty, as in slender resources or a slender chance.

clue.text: Temporary home with unusual merit

parts.note: to be in is to be at home

indicators.note: unusual means out of the ordinary, so the letters are put out of their usual order

parts.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A stopgap house that turns out to be strangely good.
explanation.definitionFit: An interim arrangement is a provisional one, lasting only until something permanent is in place.

clue.text: Old-fashioned greeting given in turn daily

indicators.note: the greeting is put inside the word for a turn

parts.note: a bend is a turn in a road
hi, an informal hello
The Times is a British daily newspaper

explanation.surface: A quaint custom of saying hello to each other in turn every day.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Daily' reads as 'every day', but it is a noun: a daily newspaper.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone behind the times is out of date, not keeping up with modern ways.

clue.text: Characteristic conclusion of pundit with comment about commercial

indicators.note: the conclusion of a word is its last letter

parts.note: the last letter of pundit

indicators.note: the comment goes about, or around, the commercial

parts.note: a remark is a comment
an ad is a commercial on TV or radio

explanation.surface: A pundit signs off with a remark about an advertisement, as usual.
explanation.walkthrough: The commercial goes inside the comment after its first letter, not around the whole thing.
explanation.definitionFit: A trademark, figuratively, is a distinctive feature or habit by which someone is recognised.

clue.text: Line in eccentric circle on china dish

indicators.note: eccentric means off-centre and odd, so the letters are thrown into a new arrangement

parts.note: L is the abbreviation for line
these thirteen letters are mixed together with the line

explanation.surface: A line painted inside a wobbly circle on a piece of porcelain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'China' looks like the country or the crockery; here it is simply letters for the mix, along with 'on'.
explanation.definitionFit: Chilli con carne is a spicy stew of minced beef, beans and chilli peppers.

clue.text: Young lion? It's distracted painter

parts.note: a cub is a young lion

indicators.note: something distracted is confused and disordered, so these letters are jumbled

parts.note: the three letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: An artist is put off by a lion cub wandering into the studio.
explanation.definitionFit: A Cubist is a painter of the Cubism movement led by Picasso and Braque.

clue.text: Change name in secret

indicators.note: the name is placed inside the word for secret

parts.note: covert means secret or hidden
N is the abbreviation for name

explanation.surface: Someone changes their name on the quiet.
explanation.definitionFit: To convert something is to transform it into a different form or belief.

clue.text: Cipher cracked by don about love

indicators.note: the rearranged letters go about, or around, the symbol for love
something cracked is broken apart, so these letters are reassembled

parts.note: the five letters to be rearranged
love is zero in tennis, which looks like O

explanation.surface: An Oxford academic breaks a secret code all about romance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cipher cracked' reads as code-breaking, but 'cracked' scrambles 'by don' into NBODY, which wraps around O.
explanation.definitionFit: A cipher is a person of no importance or influence, just as a nobody is.

clue.text: Bird from extremely cold north

parts.note: a bitter wind is extremely cold
N is the abbreviation for north

explanation.surface: A bird that has flown in from the freezing north.
explanation.definitionFit: The bittern is a heron-like wading bird of reed beds, known for its booming call.

clue.text: One in crowd scene, wide?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a film actor hired to fill out a background crowd
second meaning: in cricket, a ball bowled out of the batsman's reach, giving a run not scored off the bat

explanation.surface: A film director asks whether a crowd scene should be shot in wide angle.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket, a wide is one kind of extra, a run added to the score without the batsman hitting it; the question mark flags it as an example.
explanation.definitionFit: Extras are background actors in films, and in cricket a wide, bye or no-ball counts as an extra.

clue.text: Happy to a smaller extent inside base

indicators.note: the phrase for a smaller extent goes inside the word for base

parts.note: a bed is a base or foundation, as a bed of gravel
less means to a smaller degree

explanation.surface: Someone is less content now they are stuck at the base.
explanation.definitionFit: To be blessed is to be fortunate and joyful, close to happy in older usage.

clue.text: Good to interrupt dreadful lament

indicators.note: to interrupt is to break into the middle of something

parts.note: dire means dreadful
G is the abbreviation for good

explanation.surface: Something good breaks into a dreadful song of mourning.
explanation.definitionFit: A dirge is a mournful song or hymn sung at a funeral, a musical lament.

clue.text: Time after surface broke

indicators.note: the time comes after the other word in the final order

parts.note: skin is the outer surface
T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: Some time after it was laid, the surface cracked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Broke' looks like a past-tense verb but is the adjective. Skint is British slang for having no money.
explanation.definitionFit: Skint is informal British slang for penniless, the same sense as being broke.

clue.text: Badly need approval, giving up fine enterprise

indicators.note: badly means done wrongly, so the letters are put in a wrong order

parts.note: the four letters to be rearranged

indicators.note: giving something up means letting it go, so a letter is dropped

parts.note: to look on with favour is to approve
F is the pencil-grade abbreviation for fine

explanation.surface: Someone desperate for approval gives up a perfectly good business venture.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fine' looks like an adjective praising the enterprise; it is the letter F, dropped from FAVOUR.
explanation.definitionFit: An endeavour is an undertaking or venture, a sense shared with enterprise.

clue.text: Vigorous technique in call for attention

indicators.note: the technique sits inside the attention-getting call

parts.note: hey is a shout to catch someone's attention
an art is a skill or technique, as in the art of persuasion

explanation.surface: An energetic method for getting someone to notice you.
explanation.definitionFit: Hearty means strong and robust, as in a hearty appetite or a hearty slap on the back.

clue.text: Endlessly eager learner beginning to enjoy university

indicators.note: without an end, so the final letter is cut off

parts.note: keen means eager
L for learner, from the L-plates on a learner driver's car

indicators.note: only the opening letter of the next word is used

parts.note: the first letter of enjoy

explanation.surface: A keen student is starting to have fun at university.
explanation.walkthrough: Keele is a university in Staffordshire, in the English Midlands.
explanation.definitionFit: Keele University is a campus institution near Newcastle-under-Lyme, so it is one example of a university.
